devotions.scriptureBody:
3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
4 and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you,
5 who through faith are shielded by God’s power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time.
6 In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials
7 so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
8 Though you have not seen Him, you love Him; and though you do not see Him now, you believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy,
9 now that you are receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
devotions.application:
Before Peter mentions any trouble, he praises God for what has already been given: new birth into a living hope, an inheritance that is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,” and God’s own power shielding us along the way. That order matters on an ordinary day. So much of what we hold can slip away, like the house you grew up in, now sold to strangers. Peter points us first to what cannot be taken, because it is reserved in heaven for us.

He is honest that grief is real. Trials hurt, yet he calls them “for a little while” and says they are doing something: proving a faith more precious than gold. The long wait in a hospital hallway is not wasted in God’s hands. Then comes the wonder of verse 8. We have not seen Jesus, yet we love Him. Joy can sit right beside sorrow, not because life is easy, but because our hope is alive, rooted in His resurrection, and kept safe by God’s power until the day He is revealed.
devotions.question: What grief is weighing on you right now, and what might it look like to let a living hope stand beside it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers.
2 But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night.
3 He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does.
4 Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind.
5 Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.
6 For the LORD guards the path of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
devotions.application:
The drift in this psalm happens by degrees: walking, then setting foot on a path, then sitting down. Few people set out to become cynical. We listen a little longer to the friend who sneers at everyone and laugh along at the dinner table, until one day we find we’ve taken a seat among the mockers. The psalm doesn’t scold. It shows us where certain paths lead.

Then it offers another picture: a tree planted by streams of water. A tree doesn’t strain to grow. It stays put and drinks. That is what delighting in the Lord’s law can look like on an ordinary day: returning to it, turning a verse over while folding laundry, and letting it soak in. The fruit comes “in season,” too. There may be dry stretches at work or at home when nothing seems to be growing. Roots still matter then, and the leaf does not wither even when the harvest is months away. Chaff is light and blows wherever the wind goes, but a rooted life can stand. And the Lord Himself guards the path of the righteous, the ones who stay planted by the water.
devotions.question: Who are the voices you find yourself sitting with most often, and what would it look like to plant yourself nearer the streams of God’s word?

devotions.scriptureBody:
35 Early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray.
36 Simon and his companions went to look for Him,
37 and when they found Him, they said, “Everyone is looking for You!”
38 But Jesus answered, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.”
39 So He went throughout Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.
devotions.application:
In the verses just before this, Jesus had healed late into the evening while the whole town crowded at the door. Then, while it was still dark, He got up and went out to a solitary place to pray. It’s a freeing picture. If Jesus made room to be alone with His Father, our own need for stillness is not a weakness to apologize for.

Then Simon and his companions find Him with urgent news: “Everyone is looking for You!” That voice is familiar to anyone who has ever been needed, like a parent hearing a child call from the next room before the coffee is poured. Jesus doesn’t ignore people, but He isn’t steered by the loudest demand either. Out of that early hour of prayer comes a settled sense of what He came to do, and He moves on to the neighboring towns. Time with God doesn’t always shrink our to-do list, but it can show us which things are truly ours to carry and which we can set down. Your solitary place might be a kitchen table before sunrise or a parked car at lunch. It doesn’t need to be grand, only honest.
devotions.question: When it feels like everyone is looking for you, what might a few unhurried minutes with God help you see about what is truly yours to do?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Then the LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you.
2 I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.
3 I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
4 So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.
devotions.application:
God’s call to Abram came without a map. Leave what is familiar, He said, and go “to the land I will show you.” Not a land already shown. Abram had to set out before he could see where he was going. Few of us will leave our country for a place we have never seen, but we know the feeling. It might be agreeing to care for an aging parent in your own home, unsure how the household will change or how long it will last. Stepping forward without knowing how it ends is unsettling.

Look at what God gives Abram instead of a map: promises. I will make you, I will bless you, I will show you. The weight rests on God, not on Abram’s planning. And the blessing was never meant to stop with him: “so that you will be a blessing.” Even our uncertain steps can become good for the people around us. Then comes that small detail at the end: Abram was seventy-five when he left Haran. It is not too late to be called, or to answer. The call may not be a grand departure, only the next faithful step.
devotions.question: How might God be inviting you to step forward before you can see where it leads, and which of His promises could you lean on as you go?

devotions.scriptureBody:
13 Therefore prepare your minds for action. Be sober-minded. Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
14 As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance.
15 But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do,
16 for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”
devotions.application:
Peter’s words sound like someone rolling up their sleeves: “prepare your minds for action. Be sober-minded.” Not frantic, not fearful, just clear. The opposite is familiar enough: a mind pulled in a dozen directions at once, like trying to follow a recipe while three people talk to you. Peter doesn’t ask us to sort all of that out before breakfast. He points our hope somewhere steady, “fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.” Hope set there doesn’t have to be propped up by a good day at work or a smooth stretch at home.

From that hope comes a different way of living. The call to “be holy in all you do” can sound out of reach, but holiness here means belonging to God and coming to resemble Him, the way children pick up the ways of a parent they love. It shows up in small places: the honest answer on a timesheet, the patient word at the dinner table, the old habit we let go of without fanfare. We are not who we were. And the One who calls us to this is also the One whose grace we are waiting for.
devotions.question: Which of your words, choices, or habits might change if your hope rested fully on the grace to be given at Christ’s revelation?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands.
2 Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge.
3 Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard,
4 their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world. In the heavens He has pitched a tent for the sun.
5 Like a bridegroom emerging from his chamber, like a champion rejoicing to run his course,
6 it rises at one end of the heavens and runs its circuit to the other; nothing is deprived of its warmth.
devotions.application:
It is easy to go through a whole day with our eyes on the ground, fixed on the next task, the next conversation, or the next thing that might go wrong. Yet David reminds us that above all of it, the sky has been speaking the whole time. “Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge.” There are no words and no sound to be heard, and still the message carries. It tells of the glory of God, and it reaches a farmer in Kenya, a nurse walking to her car after a long shift in Ohio, and a child looking out a bus window in Manila.

Look at how David describes the sun. It is not a tired machine but a bridegroom stepping out with joy, a champion glad to run his course. And “nothing is deprived of its warmth.” That includes you, on the days you feel overlooked or weak. You might stop at a window or a doorway and look up for a moment. There is no need to stir up a feeling. Let the light on your face remind you that the One who pitched a tent for the sun has not forgotten the ground beneath your feet.
devotions.question: Where in your life do you feel overlooked, and what might the warmth of the sun be saying to you about the God who made it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 On one occasion, while Jesus was standing by the Lake of Gennesaret with the crowd pressing in on Him to hear the word of God,
2 He saw two boats at the edge of the lake. The fishermen had left them and were washing their nets.
3 Jesus got into the boat belonging to Simon and asked him to put out a little from shore. And sitting down, He taught the people from the boat.
4 When Jesus had finished speaking, He said to Simon, “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.”
5 “Master,” Simon replied, “we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets.”
6 When they had done so, they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to tear.
7 So they signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them, and they came and filled both boats so full that they began to sink.
8 When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees. “Go away from me, Lord,” he said, “for I am a sinful man.”
9 For he and his companions were astonished at the catch of fish they had taken,
10 and so were his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus said to Simon. “From now on you will catch men.”
11 And when they had brought their boats ashore, they left everything and followed Him.
devotions.application:
Simon was tired. He had worked hard all night with nothing to show for it, and he was already washing his nets, the work of someone ready to go home. Long, fruitless effort has its own weariness, like a conversation with a teenager that keeps ending in silence. Into that weariness, Jesus borrows Simon’s boat and then asks him to put out into deep water. Simon tells Him honestly how the night went. Then he says, “But because You say so, I will let down the nets.”

What follows is more than Simon can hold. The nets tear and the boats begin to sink, and his first response is not celebration but fear. He falls at Jesus’ knees and confesses, “I am a sinful man.” Standing so near the Lord, Simon sees his sin clearly and expects to be sent away. Yet Jesus stays. He says, “Do not be afraid,” and gives Simon a new calling. Simon’s sin is brought into the open, and Jesus does not turn from him. You can bring Him your empty nets and your sin alike, and listen for what He might say next.
devotions.question: What would it look like to bring Jesus both your empty nets and your sin, and to let down the nets again because He says so?

devotions.scriptureBody:
22 Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, love one another deeply, from a pure heart.
23 For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.
24 For, “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall,
25 but the word of the Lord stands forever.” And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.
devotions.application:
Grass withers. Flowers fall. Peter reminds his readers that everything around them fades, and the same is true for us. Careers peak and settle, bodies tire, and the things that felt urgent a month ago are often hard to remember now. That could sound bleak, but Peter means it as freedom. What God has spoken does not wither, and it is that living word that has given you new birth, a fresh start whose life comes from God Himself and will not wear out.

So what do we do with a life built on something that lasts? Peter’s answer is surprisingly ordinary: love one another deeply, from a pure heart. Not polite tolerance, but the kind of love that stays patient with a brother who restarts the same old argument at every family dinner, listens to a tired spouse, and makes the phone call to the friend who hasn’t written back in months. Much of what we chase will fall like petals. The love we give to the people in front of us, rooted in God’s enduring word, is part of what remains.
devotions.question: Who in your life might God be inviting you to love more deeply, knowing that so much else you worry about will fade?

devotions.scriptureBody:
8 “For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways,” declares the LORD.
9 “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts.
10 For just as rain and snow fall from heaven and do not return without watering the earth, making it bud and sprout, and providing seed to sow and food to eat,
11 so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please, and it will prosper where I send it.
devotions.application:
Most days we try to make sense of things by measuring them against our own plans: the job that didn’t come through, the child who isn’t calling back. When life doesn’t add up, we assume nothing is happening. Isaiah offers a different picture. God’s thoughts are as far above ours as the heavens are above the earth. That distance can be a place to rest. We don’t have to see the whole field to trust the One who sends the rain.

Rain makes little noise as it soaks into the soil. For days nothing seems to change, and then something green pushes up. God says His word works like that. The verse you read, the promise from Scripture you half-remember from years ago, the passage a friend once pointed you to: what God has spoken will not return to Him empty. It is at work in you, even on the dull and tired days, becoming seed and bread you may one day share. You may not see anything sprouting yet. Let that be enough for now: to be watered, and to wait.
devotions.question: When you are waiting to see something grow in your life, what would it look like to trust that God’s word is already at work there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 On the third day a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there,
2 and Jesus and His disciples had also been invited to the wedding.
3 When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to Him, “They have no more wine.”
4 “Woman, what is that to you and to Me?” Jesus replied. “My hour has not yet come.”
5 His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.”
6 Now six stone water jars had been set there for the Jewish rites of purification. Each could hold from twenty to thirty gallons.
7 Jesus told the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” So they filled them to the brim.
8 “Now draw some out,” He said, “and take it to the master of the banquet.” They did so,
9 and the master of the banquet tasted the water that had been turned into wine. He did not know where it was from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew. Then he called the bridegroom aside
10 and said, “Everyone serves the fine wine first, and then the cheap wine after the guests are drunk. But you have saved the fine wine until now!”
11 Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.
devotions.application:
Running out is an ordinary kind of trouble. At Cana it was wine; for you it might be patience with a parent who asks the same question for the third time in an hour. Nobody at the wedding was in danger; a family was about to be embarrassed. Yet Jesus’ mother brought even this small, awkward need to Him. She said it plainly, “They have no more wine,” and then left it with Him, telling the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.”

What He told the servants was not dramatic. Fill the jars with water. Draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet. It may have felt foolish, hauling water when the problem was wine. But they filled the jars to the brim, and they were the ones who knew where the fine wine came from. Much of faithfulness looks like that: the next plain task, done fully, while trusting Jesus with what we cannot fix. You may not see anything change. Still, you can name what has run out, do the small thing in front of you, and watch. Sometimes He saves the fine wine for later than we expect.
devotions.question: How might you name what has run out in your life, and what small, ordinary task could you do fully while you wait on Jesus?

devotions.scriptureBody:
3 Trust in the LORD and do good; dwell in the land and cultivate faithfulness.
4 Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.
5 Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it.
6 He will bring forth your righteousness like the dawn, your justice like the noonday sun.
7 Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him; do not fret when men prosper in their ways, when they carry out wicked schemes.
devotions.application:
It’s easy to read “He will give you the desires of your heart” and skip straight to the wish list. But the psalm begins on humbler ground: trust in the Lord, do good, dwell in the land, and cultivate faithfulness like a garden. Much of that happens in unremarkable places: packing lunches, keeping a promise, showing up for a friend who needs a ride. Delighting in the Lord is not a strategy for getting what we want. It is the slow way our wants begin to change as we enjoy Him.

Verse 7 knows we will be tempted to fret. Someone cuts corners, underbids you, and wins the job you priced honestly. The psalm names this plainly: people do prosper in their ways and carry out wicked schemes. Yet it invites us to be still before the Lord and wait patiently for Him, trusting that He sees and that He will bring forth our righteousness like the dawn. You could name one thing you have been gripping tightly and place it in His hands. Then return to the small, good work in front of you.
devotions.question: Which worry or wish have you been gripping most tightly, and what would committing it to the Lord and waiting patiently for Him look like?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander.
2 Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation,
3 now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.
4 As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight,
5 you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
devotions.application:
Peter’s list is uncomfortably ordinary: malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander. These aren’t dramatic sins. They’re the small jab in a group chat, the résumé detail stretched a little, the hidden sting when a friend gets the promotion, and the story about a brother-in-law repeated with a bit too much relish. Peter doesn’t just say stop. He says crave something better, the way a newborn wants milk: eagerly, hungrily, every few hours. Growth comes less from gritting our teeth than from returning again and again to the Lord we have already tasted and found good.

Then Peter points us to Jesus, the living stone, rejected by people but precious to God. If you feel overlooked at work or misunderstood at home, He knows that road. And you are not a loose brick. God is fitting you together with others into a spiritual house, and your everyday offerings—a patient answer, an honest invoice, a kind word about someone absent—become gifts He gladly receives through Christ. That is the steady work of a priest: bringing ordinary moments to God.
devotions.question: Where do malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, or slander creep most easily into your days, and what might it look like to come hungry to the Lord instead?

devotions.scriptureBody:
31 He put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man took and planted in his field.
32 Although it is the smallest of all seeds, yet it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.”
33 He told them still another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.”
devotions.application:
What matters most in a life often starts out embarrassingly small. Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, the smallest of all seeds, that a man planted in his field. It is also like leaven a woman mixed into three measures of flour. Neither looks like much at the start. The seed disappears into the dirt. The leaven vanishes into the dough. Yet the seed grows into the largest of garden plants, a tree where birds come and nest, and the leaven keeps working, unseen, until all of the flour is leavened.

That is good news on a day when your faithfulness feels too small to count. Maybe it is the ten minutes you spend helping a child sound out words at the kitchen table, or one honest sentence of prayer before a conversation you dread. Next to the weight of your own weakness, such things can seem invisible. But God is not waiting for you to do something large. He works through hidden, ordinary things, and He works over time. You may not see the growth yet. You can still plant the seed, mix in the leaven, and trust Him with the rest.
devotions.question: What small, hidden act of faithfulness could you plant and leave with God, trusting Him to grow it in His own time?

devotions.scriptureBody:
9 Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were instructing the people said to all of them, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.” For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law.
10 Then Nehemiah told them, “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”
11 And the Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve.”
12 Then all the people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, because they understood the words that had been made known to them.
devotions.application:
The people heard God’s word read aloud and wept. They may have seen how far they had drifted and how much had been lost. Their leaders didn’t scold the tears, but they did redirect them: “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.” Then came an unexpected instruction: go eat something good, drink something sweet, and make sure the neighbor with an empty table gets a share.

The weeping part can feel familiar. We open Scripture and mostly hear what we’ve gotten wrong, like the impatient reply we gave an aging parent who asked the same question twice. Honest sorrow has its place. But this passage suggests grief is not meant to be where we stay. Nehemiah’s reason was that “the joy of the LORD is your strength.” That gladness comes from Him, not from having our lives sorted out. And the joy went outward right away, with portions sent to people who had nothing prepared. There may be a small feast waiting for you, too: a shared meal, a plate carried next door, or a moment to be still and receive.
devotions.question: Who comes to mind when you read of portions sent to those with nothing prepared, and how might the Lord’s joy reach them through you?

devotions.scriptureBody:
9 But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.
10 Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
devotions.application:
We carry labels other people gave us, or ones we gave ourselves: the one who never finishes things, the disappointing child, the friend who always says the wrong thing. Peter writes to scattered, ordinary believers and hands them different names: chosen, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession. These aren’t rewards for doing well. They describe what God has done, calling people “out of darkness into His marvelous light.”

Look at the once-and-now pattern in verse 10. Once you were not a people; now you belong. Once you had not received mercy; now you have. That shift can reshape an ordinary day. A priest brings others before God, so being part of a royal priesthood might look like praying by name for the neighbor who just lost her husband, or bringing a little light into a tense family dinner. Proclaiming His virtues may be less about speeches and more about how we answer a sharp word, forgive a slight, or speak of Him when someone asks why we have hope. You belong to Him right now, before you’ve accomplished anything at all.
devotions.question: When an old label about yourself surfaces, how might your day change if you heard God call you chosen, His own, and someone who has received mercy?

devotions.scriptureBody:
5 The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure.
6 The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places; surely my inheritance is delightful.
7 I will bless the LORD who counsels me; even at night my conscience instructs me.
8 I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.
9 Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely.
10 For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.
11 You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand.
devotions.application:
It is easy to measure a life by what we hold, the way a farmer counts the harvest stacked in his barn. David starts somewhere else. “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup.” Before he names any blessing, he names God as what he has. Other things in his hands may change, but that will not.

David’s days were not easy. He speaks of nights when his conscience is still instructing him, and he knows the grave is real. But he has formed a habit: “I have set the LORD always before me.” It is a choice made again and again, at the kitchen table or in the car before a hard conversation. With the Lord at his right hand, close as a friend at his side, he is not shaken. Even the grave will not keep him, for God will not abandon his soul to it. Christians have long heard in verse 10 a promise kept when Jesus rose. So the path ahead leads toward joy in God’s presence. When your eyes drift elsewhere, you can turn them gently back to Him.
devotions.question: How do you tend to steady yourself when a day feels uncertain, and what might change if you set the Lord before you first?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Then Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through.
2 And there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy.
3 He was trying to see who Jesus was, but could not see over the crowd because he was small in stature.
4 So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was about to pass that way.
5 When Jesus came to that place, He looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.”
6 So Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully.
7 And all who saw this began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!”
8 But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.”
9 Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham.
10 For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
devotions.application:
Zacchaeus had money, a title, and a reputation that entered rooms before he did. None of it helped him see Jesus. So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree, hardly a dignified thing for a wealthy man to do. That mix of longing and awkwardness can feel familiar: wanting to see Jesus, yet feeling too small for the crowd or too well known for your failures.

But it is Jesus who looks up first. He stops beneath the tree, calls Zacchaeus by name, and says He must stay at his house today. The crowd grumbles, as people still do when someone’s past seems too heavy to welcome. Jesus goes anyway. Only after that welcome does Zacchaeus open his hands: half his possessions to the poor, fourfold to anyone he cheated. The change follows the welcome; it does not purchase it. You may be the one up in the tree, hoping to be seen, or the one below, muttering about who deserves a seat at the table. Either way, Jesus came to seek and to save the lost, and He knows your name.
devotions.question: Which part of your life—your money, your home, or a strained relationship—might Jesus be inviting you to open gladly in response to His welcome?

devotions.scriptureBody:
14 Now, therefore, fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth; cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.
15 But if it is unpleasing in your sight to serve the LORD, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!”
devotions.application:
Joshua stands before a people who have already crossed the river and settled in the land, and still he asks them to choose. Faith, it seems, is not decided once and filed away. It is chosen again, “this day.” Look at the two kinds of gods he names: the old ones their fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and the gods of the Amorites in whose land they are living. We know both. There are the patterns we inherited, like the way our family met every disappointment with silence. And there are the gods of the place we live now, such as the steady pull to be admired.

Joshua sets the choice in the open, then tells his own: “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!” Serving the Lord “in sincerity and truth” happens in small places: the tone we use at the dinner table, the apology we finally offer, the trust we place in Him when the way ahead is unclear. You might take a few moments to name what asks for your loyalty, and remember that Joshua’s choice can become yours, made fresh each day.
devotions.question: Where do the habits you inherited or the pressures of the place you live now ask for your loyalty, and what would serving the Lord in sincerity look like there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
8 Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble.
9 Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.
10 For, “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech.
11 He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it.
12 For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”
devotions.application:
Few days bring dramatic conflict. More often it is something small, like a brother who answers your careful question with a sigh and a remark about how you always overthink things. Peter knows how natural it feels to answer insult with insult. It can even feel fair. But he points another way: repay evil not with evil, but “with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.” The hurt is real, yet we are people headed toward blessing, and we are invited to pass it along on the way.

Blessing is often small. It might mean holding back the clever reply, refusing to repeat the story that makes someone look bad, or offering a kind word to the person who wasn’t kind first. Peter says to “seek peace and pursue it,” which suggests peace rarely just shows up. Sometimes we have to go after it. And none of this happens unseen. Peter reminds us that “the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer.” When you hold back a harsh word or choose tenderness over winning, God sees it, and He is listening.
devotions.question: What would it look like to answer someone who has recently hurt or irritated you with blessing rather than a matching reply?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 A Psalm of David, when he was in the Wilderness of Judah. O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water.
2 So I have seen You in the sanctuary and beheld Your power and glory.
3 Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You.
4 So I will bless You as long as I live; in Your name I will lift my hands.
5 My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods; with joyful lips my mouth will praise You.
6 When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night.
7 For You are my help; I will sing for joy in the shadow of Your wings.
8 My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me.
devotions.application:
David wrote this psalm in the Wilderness of Judah, “a dry and weary land without water.” He did not wait for the desert to end before he prayed. Your dry place might be a long season of caring for a parent who no longer remembers your name, or a stretch when God feels far away. Even there, David says, “O God, You are my God.” His thirst itself becomes a kind of prayer. He also reaches back to what he has seen of God’s power and glory in the sanctuary. When the present feels empty, remembering can steady us.

And when sleep will not come, David does not only rehearse his worries. He thinks of God “through the watches of the night,” those long hours before dawn. Lying awake can become a place of meeting rather than only dread. Look at the last line, too. David’s soul clings, but it is God’s right hand that upholds him. Your grip may feel weak right now. That is all right. You are held by a hand stronger than your own, and God’s loving devotion is better than life itself.
devotions.question: Who is God to you in your own dry and weary land, and how might you tell Him plainly that you thirst for Him there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
46 Next, they came to Jericho. And as Jesus and His disciples were leaving Jericho with a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, was sitting beside the road.
47 When he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
48 Many people admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
49 Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man. “Take courage!” they said. “Get up! He is calling for you.”
50 Throwing off his cloak, Bartimaeus jumped up and came to Jesus.
51 “What do you want Me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “Rabboni,” said the blind man, “let me see again.”
52 “Go,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you.” And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road.
devotions.application:
Bartimaeus sat beside the road, the place where people end up when life has moved on without them. You may know something of that spot, like the long stretch after a friendship cooled and the invitations stopped coming. When he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing, he cried out for mercy, and many people told him to be silent. Voices still say that. Don’t bother anyone. Keep it together. Your need is too much. Bartimaeus cried out all the louder, and Jesus stopped.

Then Jesus asked, “What do you want Me to do for you?” He surely knew, yet He invited the man to name it plainly. You can do the same, standing at the kitchen sink or wherever you are, with no polished words. Bartimaeus threw off his cloak, perhaps the one thing he owned, and jumped up to come. Once he could see, he followed Jesus along the road. Whatever your answer looks like, the invitation stands: come close, and keep walking with Him.
devotions.question: When Jesus stops beside your road and asks, “What do you want Me to do for you?” what would you honestly tell Him?

devotions.scriptureBody:
13 Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good?
14 But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. “Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken.”
15 But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect,
16 keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ.
17 For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.
devotions.application:
Peter writes to people who were being misunderstood and talked about for their faith, and he doesn’t promise them an easy road. He says something steadier: even if you suffer for what is right, you are blessed. Fear is real, but it does not have to rule you. Your fear might be as small as staying silent when a friend at dinner jokes about people who pray. Peter’s answer begins inside: “in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord.” That means setting Him apart and giving Him the central place, the seat that worry keeps trying to take.

From that settled place, something else becomes possible. When someone asks why you still have hope, you don’t need a polished speech or a winning argument. You can tell them honestly, with gentleness and respect. Peter cares as much about how we answer as about what we say. A kind tone, a clear conscience, and steady good behavior often speak louder than any debate. You may be misread for a while, and it may cost you something. Still, Peter reminds us that it is better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.
devotions.question: How would it change the way you respond to doubt or mockery if Christ, not fear, held the central place in your heart?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD:
2 “Go down at once to the potter’s house, and there I will give you My message.”
3 So I went down to the potter’s house and saw him working at the wheel.
4 But the vessel that he was shaping from the clay became flawed in his hand; so he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do.
5 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
6 “O house of Israel, declares the LORD, can I not treat you as this potter treats his clay? Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel.
devotions.application:
Jeremiah walked down to the potter’s house and watched a man at work. The wheel turned, the potter’s hands shaped the clay, and something went wrong. The vessel became flawed right there in his hand. What the potter did next is worth pausing over: he didn’t throw the clay away. He formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do.

It is a familiar feeling to be flawed in the middle of being shaped. Think of a friendship that cracked over one careless remark and has never sat quite right since. God’s word to Israel here was not soft. It reminded them that He has every right to reshape His people, and reshaping can be uncomfortable. But look where the clay stays the whole time: in the potter’s hand. Whatever feels misshapen in you is not beyond His reach. It may be the very place where His hands are still at work, forming something you cannot yet see.
devotions.question: Which part of your life feels flawed or unfinished right now, and what might change if you pictured it still resting in God’s hand?

devotions.scriptureBody:
15 When they had finished eating, Jesus asked Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus replied, “Feed My lambs.”
16 Jesus asked a second time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus told him, “Shepherd My sheep.”
17 Jesus asked a third time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” “Lord, You know all things,” he replied. “You know I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep.
18 Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.”
19 Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after He had said this, He told him, “Follow Me.”
devotions.application:
When they had finished eating, Jesus turned to Simon Peter. Not long before, Peter had insisted he would never fall away. Then, warming himself beside another fire, he said three times that he did not know Jesus. Now Jesus asks three times, “Do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt, and some questions do hurt. Yet Jesus does not demand an explanation or recite Peter’s failures. He asks about love, and then He hands Peter work to do: “Feed My lambs.” “Shepherd My sheep.”

You may carry a failure that still stings: a sharp word to your child, a broken promise, or a moment you kept silent when you should have spoken up. Jesus does not restore Peter by acting as if the denial never happened. He brings him back into love and back into usefulness. Your sheep might be a neighbor recovering from surgery, an aging parent, or a friend in a hard season. And when the road ahead leads where you do not want to go, through illness, age, or the loss of control, His word to you is the same plain one He spoke to Peter: “Follow Me.”
devotions.question: Where does an old failure still sting, and as Jesus asks whether you love Him, whom might He be calling you to care for?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. A Psalm of the sons of Korah. How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of Hosts!
2 My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God.
3 Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she places her young near Your altars, O LORD of Hosts, my King and my God.
4 How blessed are those who dwell in Your house! They are ever praising You. Selah
5 Blessed are those whose strength is in You, whose hearts are set on pilgrimage.
6 As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs; even the autumn rain covers it with pools.
7 They go from strength to strength, until each appears before God in Zion.
8 O LORD God of Hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob. Selah
9 Take notice of our shield, O God, and look with favor on the face of Your anointed.
10 For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked.
11 For the LORD God is a sun and a shield; the LORD gives grace and glory; He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity.
12 O LORD of Hosts, how blessed is the man who trusts in You!
devotions.application:
The longing in this psalm can feel far from an ordinary day. Yet the psalmist names something that runs beneath the busyness: a soul that “longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD.” Look at the sparrow and the swallow. Small, common birds found a home near God’s altars and raised their young there. There is room for you too, with your unfinished work and your tired heart.

The psalm is honest that the road has dry stretches. Pilgrims still pass through the Valley of Baca, a name that likely echoes weeping. But those whose strength is in the Lord “make it a place of springs,” and the autumn rain covers it with pools. Your valley might be the long season of driving an aging father to appointments he no longer remembers. You are not asked to produce your own strength. Pilgrims go “from strength to strength” as God supplies it, and He meets them on the way. He is “a sun and a shield,” and He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity.
devotions.question: What dry valley are you walking through right now, and what would it look like to let your strength be in God there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
7 The end of all things is near. Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray.
8 Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins.
9 Show hospitality to one another without complaining.
10 As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another.
11 If anyone speaks, he should speak as one conveying the words of God. If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
devotions.application:
Peter opens with words that sound urgent: “The end of all things is near.” Yet look at what he does with that urgency. He doesn’t tell anyone to panic or to scan the world for signs. He says, “be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray.” When worries run ahead of us and our thoughts scatter, a settled mind is a gift. It makes room for prayer again.

Then Peter turns to the ordinary. Love one another deeply. Welcome people without complaining. Use what you’ve been given. Love that “covers over a multitude of sins” might look like choosing not to replay an old family argument one more time. Hospitality might be a pot of soup carried to a neighbor after a long week, offered without sighing about the dishes. And whatever you’re good at, whether listening, fixing things, teaching, or organizing, was entrusted to you the way a steward manages someone else’s household: to care for and to share. You don’t have to serve out of your own thin reserves. Peter says to serve “with the strength God provides,” so that God receives the glory through Jesus Christ.
devotions.question: Who near you could be served by the gift God has entrusted to you, if you leaned on the strength He provides rather than your own?

devotions.scriptureBody:
13 Someone in the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
14 But Jesus replied, “Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?”
15 And He said to them, “Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.”
16 Then He told them a parable: “The ground of a certain rich man produced an abundance.
17 So he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?’
18 Then he said, ‘This is what I will do: I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones, and there I will store up all my grain and my goods.
19 Then I will say to myself, “You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry!”’
20 But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’
21 This is how it will be for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.”
devotions.application:
It starts with a family argument over an inheritance, the kind of thing that can still divide brothers and sisters. Jesus doesn’t settle the dispute; He goes underneath it, reminding the crowd that “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” He tells them to guard themselves against “every form of greed.” That reaches past the hunger for more money. It can be the running tally of what we think we’re owed, the worry that makes us grip tighter, or the hope that one more good year will finally let us rest.

See how lonely the rich man is. He thinks to himself, talks to himself, plans for himself. No one else appears in his story, not a neighbor and not God. Planning ahead isn’t the problem. His life has shrunk to the size of his barns. Being rich toward God can look ordinary: sharing a harvest of tomatoes with the widower down the street, giving an hour to a friend, letting go of an old grudge over money, or pausing to thank God for what is already enough. Our days rest in His hands, not in what we manage to store up.
devotions.question: When you catch yourself planning bigger barns, what would it look like to become rich toward God in the choices in front of you?

devotions.scriptureBody:
17 Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls,
18 yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!
19 GOD the Lord is my strength; He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights! For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments.
devotions.application:
Habakkuk lists everything his people depended on: figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, and cattle. This was their paycheck, their pantry, and their retirement, and one by one he imagines it all gone. You could write your own version of that list. “Though the small business I poured ten years into is closing its doors…” Then comes one small word: yet. Habakkuk is honest that the fields are empty. He doesn’t wait for the harvest to return before he rejoices. He finds his joy in the Lord Himself, “the God of my salvation,” rather than in what God provides. That isn’t denial. It is a trust that runs deeper than circumstances.

Look, too, at what God gives him. He doesn’t flatten the mountain. He makes Habakkuk’s feet like those of a deer, sure and steady on rocky, high places. That is strength for the climb, not a promise that there will be no climb. And this prayer was handed to the choirmaster, set to stringed instruments for the whole community to sing. Whatever your fields look like right now, you don’t have to find your “yet” alone.
devotions.question: How would you finish Habakkuk’s “Though…” for your own life, and what might it look like to say, “yet I will exult in the LORD”?

devotions.scriptureBody:
6 Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you.
7 Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.
devotions.application:
Peter puts two things side by side that we usually keep apart: humbling ourselves and handing over our worries. They belong together, because so much of our anxiety comes from trying to hold up what was never ours to carry. We rehearse a hard conversation before it happens, or lie awake replaying a child’s choices or a friend’s long silence. Underneath it all is often an unspoken belief that if we stop gripping, everything will fall apart.

To humble yourself under God’s mighty hand is to admit that you are not that hand. Then comes the gentle invitation: “Cast all your anxiety on Him.” All of it, the small, embarrassing worries along with the respectable ones. Peter’s reason is not that you have earned God’s attention. It is “because He cares for you.” The lifting up he speaks of comes “in due time,” which means you may not see it yet. Still, you can open your hands, name what is weighing on you, and let the One who cares for you hold it.
devotions.question: Which worry are you gripping because, deep down, you believe everything depends on you, and what would it look like to place it in God’s care?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 A Psalm. A song for the dedication of the temple. Of David. I will exalt You, O LORD, for You have lifted me up and have not allowed my foes to rejoice over me.
2 O LORD my God, I cried to You for help, and You healed me.
3 O LORD, You pulled me up from Sheol; You spared me from descending into the Pit.
4 Sing to the LORD, O you His saints, and praise His holy name.
5 For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime. Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning.
devotions.application:
David writes this song looking back. He remembers crying out, standing near the edge, and being lifted up. The psalm is honest that the hard night really happened. “Weeping may stay the night” admits that grief sometimes moves in and unpacks its bags. You may know that kind of night yourself, perhaps a rift with a grown child that no phone call has mended yet.

The psalm doesn’t rush you out of that night. But it does tell you the night is not all there is. God’s favor, David says, lasts a lifetime, and joy has a way of arriving with the morning, sometimes slowly, like light easing through a window. This may be a day for crying out, as David did, without polished words. Or it may be a day to remember a time you were lifted and to thank God for it out loud. Either way, you are invited to sing with the saints, which here means all of God’s people, ordinary people who have learned that sorrow, however real, does not have the final say.
devotions.question: Where are you waiting through a long night right now, and what might it look like to cry out to the Lord honestly until morning comes?

devotions.scriptureBody:
16 I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek.
17 For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.”
devotions.application:
Paul writes as he hopes to bring the gospel to Rome, the proud capital of the empire, where news of a crucified Jewish teacher could sound foolish. Still he says, “I am not ashamed of the gospel.” His confidence does not rest on a bold temperament or clever arguments. It rests on what the gospel is: “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.” The good news is not his to prop up. When we hesitate to speak of Jesus, this frees us too: the gospel’s strength never depended on our polish.

Paul adds that the gospel reveals the righteousness of God, His way of setting people right with Himself, and that it comes by faith “from start to finish.” It is not faith to get started and then our own strength to keep going. The same trust that first drew you near can carry you through an ordinary afternoon, like sitting beside an aging parent who no longer remembers your name. “The righteous will live by faith” speaks to this day. You can lean, once more, on the God whose power was never yours to supply.
devotions.question: What makes you hesitate to speak of Jesus, and what might change if you trusted the power of God rather than your own?
